metadata.title: Do intercultural education and attitudes promote student wellbeing and social outcomes? An examination across PISA countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2018 cross-national microdata (15-year-olds) and applies PISA-provided final survey weights in all multilevel models. The authors normalize weights within each country so that the sum of weights equals that country’s sample size, which preserves country representativeness while enabling pooled estimation. They fit multilevel models with random intercepts for school and country (L1 student, L2 school, L3 country), which aligns with the nested sampling structure of PISA. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), but it does explicitly state that multilevel models are weighted, so standard errors should reflect the complex design as implemented by the weighting approach.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used publicly available PISA 2018 dataset (80 countries/economic regions) and removed countries where scale scores were not provided for any predictor variables or for all outcome variables (due to non-administration or poor internal consistency), to avoid non-random missingness. Applied multiple imputations to handle remaining missing data, using school as the cluster variable to create 10 imputations. For outcomes where some countries had 100% missing data, those countries were removed prior to analyses for those outcomes, resulting in varying sample sizes by outcome. Teacher-attitude analyses were repeated for the subset of countries where teacher-reported information was collected.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted multilevel model (L1 student, L2 school, L3 country). Student-reported intercultural practices: β=0.12 (95% CI [0.11, 0.12], p<.05). Principal-reported intercultural practices: β=-0.01 (95% CI [-0.01, 0.00], p<.05). Student-reported teacher attitudes: β=-0.04 (95% CI [-0.05, -0.03], p<.05). Teacher self-reported attitudes: β=-0.01 (95% CI [-0.02, 0.01], not meaningful). Immigrant status effects: second-gen β=-0.02 (p<.05), first-gen β=-0.03 (p<.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data (15-year-olds) with eudaimonia as the WLE-based outcome, the study leveraged student intercultural education practices and student-reported teacher attitudes (along with immigrant status and student covariates) to predict eudaimonia, finding that student-perceived intercultural education practices had a small but significant positive association (β=0.12) while principal-reported practices and teacher-reported attitudes were near zero. This indicates that strengthening students’ lived experiences of intercultural learning in school may support eudaimonic wellbeing more than relying on principals’ or teachers’ self-reports, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds), wellbeing: life satisfaction (single-item slider, WLE framework for scaling)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted multilevel model. Student-reported intercultural practices: β=0.11 (95% CI [0.10, 0.11], p<.05). Principal-reported intercultural practices: β=0.00 (95% CI [-0.01, 0.00], not meaningful). Student-reported teacher attitudes: β=0.04 (95% CI [0.03, 0.05], p<.05). Teacher self-reported attitudes: β=0.01 (95% CI [0.00, 0.02], not meaningful). Immigrant status effects: second-gen β=-0.07 (p<.05), first-gen β=-0.10 (p<.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data (15-year-olds) with life satisfaction as the outcome, the study leveraged student intercultural education practices and student-reported teacher attitudes (along with immigrant status and student covariates) to predict life satisfaction, finding that student-perceived intercultural education practices had a small but significant positive association (β=0.11) while principal-reported practices were essentially null. This indicates that policies should focus on ensuring students actually experience intercultural education activities, as student perceptions—not administrative reports—align with higher life satisfaction, though causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional associations.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds), wellbeing: positive affect (WLE scale scores)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted multilevel model. Student-reported intercultural practices: β=0.11 (95% CI [0.11, 0.11], p<.05). Principal-reported intercultural practices: β=0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.01], not meaningful). Student-reported teacher attitudes: β=0.02 (95% CI [0.01, 0.03], p<.05). Teacher self-reported attitudes: β=0.01 (95% CI [0.00, 0.02], not meaningful). Immigrant status effects: second-gen β=-0.05 (p<.05), first-gen β=-0.09 (p<.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data (15-year-olds) with positive affect as the WLE-based outcome, the study leveraged student intercultural education practices and student-reported teacher attitudes (plus immigrant status and student covariates) to predict positive affect, finding that student-perceived intercultural education practices showed a small significant positive association (β=0.11) while principal-reported practices and teacher self-reports were near zero. This indicates that improving students’ direct engagement with intercultural learning may be a practical lever for enhancing positive affect, though the study’s observational, cross-sectional nature prevents causal interpretation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds), social outcomes: school belonging (WLE scale scores)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted multilevel model. Student-reported intercultural practices: β=0.07 (95% CI [0.06, 0.07], p<.05). Principal-reported intercultural practices: β=0.00 (95% CI [-0.01, 0.00], not meaningful). Student-reported teacher attitudes: β=0.08 (95% CI [0.07, 0.09], p<.05). Teacher self-reported attitudes: β=0.02 (95% CI [0.01, 0.03], p<.05 but small). Immigrant status effects: second-gen β=-0.04 (p<.05), first-gen β=-0.12 (p<.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data (15-year-olds) with school belonging as the WLE-based outcome, the study leveraged student-perceived intercultural education practices and student-reported teacher intercultural attitudes (along with immigrant status and student covariates) to predict belonging, finding that both student-reported intercultural practices (β=0.07) and student-perceived teacher attitudes (β=0.08) were small but significant predictors. This indicates that interventions should prioritize the student experience of intercultural education and teacher attitudes to strengthen belonging, while recognizing that cross-sectional associations cannot establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds), social outcomes: victimization frequency (WLE framework for scale scores)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted multilevel model. Student-reported intercultural practices: β=-0.02 (95% CI [-0.02, -0.01], p<.05). Principal-reported intercultural practices: β=0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.01], not meaningful). Student-reported teacher attitudes: β=-0.21 (95% CI [-0.22, -0.20], p<.05). Teacher self-reported attitudes: β=0.01 (95% CI [0.00, 0.02], not meaningful). Immigrant status effects: second-gen β=0.01 (p<.05, small), first-gen β=0.03 (p<.05, small).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data (15-year-olds) with victimization as the outcome, the study leveraged student-perceived intercultural education practices and student-reported teacher intercultural attitudes (plus immigrant status and student covariates) to predict victimization, finding that student-reported intercultural practices had a trivial negative association (β=-0.02) while student-reported teacher attitudes showed a medium negative association (β=-0.21). This indicates that reducing bullying risk may depend more on students’ perceptions of teachers’ intercultural stance than on principals’ reported practices, though the observational design means these results should guide hypotheses for future causal or longitudinal work.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 cross-national data on 15-year-olds across up to 80 countries/economic regions to examine whether intercultural education practices and teachers’ intercultural attitudes are associated with wellbeing (eudaimonia, life satisfaction, positive affect) and social outcomes (school belonging, victimization). The authors fit weighted three-level multilevel models (students within schools within countries) and apply multiple imputation (10 imputations) for missing questionnaire data, combining results via Rubin’s rules. Across outcomes, the strongest and most consistent associations come from student perceptions: student-reported intercultural education practices predict higher wellbeing and belonging (e.g., β≈0.07–0.12) and slightly lower victimization (β≈-0.02), while student-reported teacher intercultural attitudes show a medium negative association with victimization (β=-0.21) and a small positive association with belonging (β=0.08). Principal- and teacher self-reports are mostly near zero. Because the design is cross-sectional and the models are not ML predictive pipelines, the findings support correlational policy guidance rather than causal claims.
